column1: # Settings of the edge image: the single source of truth for their defaults, the start-up check and SECURITY: summary
# (docker-entrypoint.d/05-kickedro-settings.envsh), the variables the templates may use (18-kickedro-render.sh), and
# One setting per line: seven fields separated by one TAB each, none empty. Lines starting with "#" and empty lines
#   DEFAULT      value used when the variable is unset or empty
#   ALLOWED      accepted values: alternatives separated by "|", each a literal value or one of these forms:
#                  <integer>  a whole number from 1, at most 15 digits
#                  <time>     a whole number from 1 with the unit ms, s, m or h, e.g. 10s
#                  <buffers>  a count and a size separated by one space, e.g. 4 8k (size in bytes, or with k or m)
#                  <path>     an absolute file path (letters, digits and . _ / - only)
#   WEAKER_IF    which values are weaker than the default; each prints one SECURITY: line at start:
#                  -          none (no value is less secure than another)
#                  >X         a value above X: numbers by value, times by duration, buffers when the count or the
#   RISK_TEXT    the protection lost by weakening (the SECURITY: line, and "If you weaken it" in the docs)
#   WHEN         when you might change it (docs)

column5: Attacks are no longer blocked: DetectionOnly only logs them, Off does not even inspect requests.
column6: ModSecurity's rule engine: On inspects requests and blocks attacks, DetectionOnly inspects and logs only, Off switches the WAF off.
column7: DetectionOnly for a first period on a new site, to find false positives in the audit log before blocking.

column5: No weaker value: 1 is the lowest level. Higher levels block more attacks and cause more false positives.
column6: OWASP CRS blocking paranoia level: how many and how strict the rules that block are.
column7: Raise it for sites that handle sensitive data, after adding exclusions for the extra false positives.

column5: A request must match more rules before it is blocked, so attacks that match only one or two rules get through.
column6: OWASP CRS inbound anomaly score threshold: a request is blocked when its matched rules add up to this score (one critical match scores 5).
column7: Briefly, while tuning a site with many false positives; narrow exclusions in custom.d are better.

column5: Responses that leak data (error messages, source code, directory listings) must match more rules before they are blocked.
column6: OWASP CRS outbound anomaly score threshold for responses.
column7: When normal responses of an application match outbound rules that cannot be excluded narrowly.

column5: Larger request bodies are accepted and buffered for inspection, which costs memory and disk and eases denial of service.
column6: Largest request body, file uploads included, in bytes (default 128 MiB); a larger body is refused.
column7: Raise it for sites that take larger uploads; lower it for sites that never do.

column5: Blocked and suspicious requests are no longer recorded: no trace of attacks, and block page references cannot be looked up.
column6: Where ModSecurity writes its audit log (blocked requests and other relevant transactions): a file, /dev/stdout (in docker logs), or off.
column7: A file on a mounted, rotated volume when docker logs are not kept or are hard to parse.

column5: No security effect: both formats record the same transactions.
column6: Audit log format: one JSON object per transaction, or ModSecurity's native multi-part format.
column7: Native when your log tooling expects it.

column5: No security effect: every allowed status refuses the request. With 444 nginx closes the connection without a response, so there is no block page.
column6: HTTP status of a response to a request ModSecurity blocks.
column7: To match what clients or monitoring expect, or 444 to send scanners nothing at all.

column5: The exact nginx version appears in the Server header and on error pages, which helps attackers pick known vulnerabilities.
column6: Whether the nginx version appears in the Server header and on nginx's error pages (nginx's server_tokens).

column5: The X-Powered-By, Server, X-AspNet-Version and X-AspNetMvc-Version headers of backends reach clients and reveal their software and versions.
column6: Removes X-Powered-By, Server, X-AspNet-Version and X-AspNetMvc-Version from backend responses (proxied, FastCGI, uWSGI and gRPC).
column7: When a client depends on one of these headers.

column5: Responses lose X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and X-Frame-Options: MIME sniffing, full URLs in referrers to other sites, and clickjacking through frames become possible again.
column6: Adds X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin and X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN to every response, error pages included, unless it already has that header (from the backend or the vhost). Also on vhosts that add headers of their own (HSTS), through nginx's add_header_inherit merge.
column7: When all applications send these headers themselves and you want nginx's stock add_header inheritance.

column5: Clients may take longer to send the request headers, so slow-header attacks (Slowloris) hold connections longer.
column6: Time a client has to send the complete request line and headers.
column7: For clients on very slow or unreliable links.

column5: Clients may pause longer while sending a request body, so slow-body attacks hold connections longer.
column6: Longest pause between two reads of the request body (not the time for the whole upload).
column7: For uploads over very slow or unreliable links.

column5: Clients that read responses very slowly hold connections and buffers longer.
column6: Longest pause between two writes of the response to the client (not the time for the whole download).
column7: For clients on very slow or unreliable links.

column5: Idle keep-alive connections stay open longer and take connection slots that an attacker can exhaust.
column6: How long an idle keep-alive connection stays open; 0 disables keep-alive.
column7: For clients that make requests with long pauses in between, such as a load balancer that reuses connections.

column5: Longer request lines and headers are accepted, which costs memory per connection and eases denial of service.
column6: Number and size of the buffers for long request lines and headers; a longer request line or header field is refused (414 or 400).
column7: When an application uses very long URLs or very large cookies.

column5: No security effect: with off, nginx's plain error page is sent, without a reference. Neither page shows rule details.
column6: A request ModSecurity blocks gets a short page with a reference: the request ID, which is also the transaction ID of its audit log entry. Other error pages nginx itself sends with the deny status (for example for deny rules) get it too. A file mounted at /etc/nginx/kickedro/block-page.html (at most 32 KiB) replaces the built-in page; {{request_id}} in it is replaced by the reference.
column7: Off when the clients are programs that do not show pages.

column5: No security effect by itself: the zones limit nothing until a vhost uses them, and a vhost that uses them stops nginx from starting when they are off.
column6: Defines the rate-limit zones kickedro_perip_10rs (10 requests per second per client address) and kickedro_login_1rs (1 per second) for limit_req in vhost snippets; applied nowhere by default.
column7: Off to save their shared memory (10 MB each) when no vhost uses them.
